module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Factorial primes

A factorial prime is a prime that is one more or one less than a factorial. It
is conjectured that there are infinitely many factorial primes.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Factorial prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorial_prime)
- [OEIS A088054](https://oeis.org/A088054)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace FactorialPrime

/-- A factorial prime is a prime one above or one below a factorial. -/
def IsFactorialPrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ ∃ n : ℕ, p = n.factorial + 1 ∨ n.factorial = p + 1

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem seven_isFactorialPrime : IsFactorialPrime 7 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 3, Or.inl ?_⟩
  norm_num

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem twentyThree_isFactorialPrime : IsFactorialPrime 23 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 4, Or.inr ?_⟩
  norm_num

/-- There are infinitely many factorial primes. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinitely_many_factorial_primes :
    Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | IsFactorialPrime p} := by
  sorry

end FactorialPrime

reformulations.difference: "One less than a factorial" is written `n.factorial = p + 1`, not `p = n! - 1`. The conjecture is stated as infinitude of the set of primes p (with n = 0 allowed), not as infinitely many n for which n! ± 1 is prime.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The two encodings of "one less" agree: n! ≥ 1 gives n! = p + 1 ⇔ p = n! − 1, and primality rules out the truncated case p = 0. Allowing n = 0 adds nothing: 0! + 1 = 2 = 1! + 1, and 0! − 1 = 0 is not prime. Counting primes and counting indices n give the same infinitude: n ↦ n! is at most 2-to-1, and n! ± 1 ≥ n − 1 is unbounded in n. Proved in scratch: `{p | IsFactorialPrime p}.Infinite ↔ {n | (n.factorial + 1).Prime ∨ (n.factorial - 1).Prime}.Infinite`. Also proved: `{p | IsFactorialPrime p}` is exactly the set of primes of the form n! + 1 together with those of the form n! − 1. Both compile against the built module.

sources_consulted: https://web.archive.org/web/20251226150851id_/https://oeis.org/A088054 (OEIS A088054 entry, Dec 2025 snapshot; oeis.org itself served a Cloudflare challenge)
review.notes:
No findings. I checked each declaration:

- `IsFactorialPrime` matches Wikipedia ("a prime number that is one less or one more than a factorial") and OEIS A088054 ("primes which are within 1 of a factorial number"). In Lean it holds for 2, 3, 5, 7, 23, 719 and 5039, and fails for 0, 1, 11 and 25.
- The two tests are correct (7 = 3! + 1, 23 = 4! − 1) and do not use `sorry`.
- `infinitely_many_factorial_primes` states exactly the conjecture the cited Wikipedia page poses. It appears only in the infobox: `con_number = Infinite`, which the template renders as "Conjectured no. of terms: Infinite".
- `research open` is correct. Wikipedia (June 2025) lists 53 known terms and says no others are known. No source records a proof or disproof.

Two related conjectures are not formalized; neither omission is a defect:
- The Prime Glossary (t5k.org), which the file does not cite, conjectures infinitely many primes of *each* form, n! + 1 and n! − 1. That is stronger than the file's union statement.
- An OEIS A088054 comment conjectures that n = 3 is the only n for which both n! − 1 and n! + 1 are prime (A002981 ∩ A002982 = {3}).

Either could be added as a variant.

I did not modify the checkout; the file under review matches HEAD. `lakefile.toml` and `run/` were already changed before this review, by the sandbox setup.
